Recent work supports text augmentation but highlights two risks. AlterRec (2024 preprint; 2025 publication) finds that simple ID/text fusion can undertrain the text component because ID features dominate; its independently trained networks do not fit this task’s single-model constraint. [AlterRec](https://aclanthology.org/2025.ijcnlp-long.12/). UniT (2025) finds that text representations can cluster excessively, particularly for less-popular items, and introduces sequence- and popularity-aware pairwise repulsion. This suggests semantic similarity alone may miss specific behavioral connections. [UniT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13530). ST2SI (2025) explicitly aligns item text with item IDs to learn transitions, but uses an LLM rather than a lightweight encoder trained from scratch. [ST2SI](https://aclanthology.org/2025.coling-main.171/).

The retrieved evidence does not establish the exact proposed configuration: BERT4Rec with a small, randomly initialized title/description encoder jointly optimized on sparse interactions. A plausible experiment, inferred from these findings, is a shared token-embedding pooler plus projection, integrated with item-ID embeddings inside one BERT4Rec network and trained through masked-item cross-entropy. Shared words could transfer interaction gradients between related items; learned ID residuals could preserve distinctions between similar descriptions. Monitor text-branch gradients and representation collapse to detect ineffective fusion. Remove both item identity and its text at masked positions, then use appended-mask inference, preserving BERT4Rec’s target-hiding principle. Benefits under the pinned validation protocol remain unverified. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690).
